html:
A light-emitting diode that gives bright blue light, first made practical in Japan in the early 1990s. Red and green LEDs had existed for decades, but blue was the missing colour, and without it LEDs could not make white light.

The key material was gallium nitride. At Nagoya, Isamu Akasaki and Hiroshi Amano learned to grow good crystals of it in the late 1980s. In 1993 Shuji Nakamura, working at the small chemical firm Nichia, made a bright, cheap blue LED that could be mass produced. He later sued Nichia for a fair share of the profits and moved to the United States.

Coat a blue LED with a yellow phosphor and it shines white. That made LED lamps possible: they use a fraction of the power of the light bulbs that followed Thomas Edison, and they now light homes, phone screens and streets. The three men shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2014.
